Direct Knowledge Transfer
for Offline QQ-Learning

Zhanye Luo ††thanks: Faculty of Business and Economics, The University of Hong Kong. Email: zhanye.luo@connect.hku.hk.    Guangyan Gan ††thanks: Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. Email: GUANGYAN001@e.ntu.edu.sg.    Lin William Cong ††thanks: Corresponding author. Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. Email: will.cong@ntu.edu.sg.
Abstract

Data-driven sequential decision making in marketing and healthcare can benefit from observations collected in related environments, particularly when data in the environment of interest are limited. Transferring such information requires accounting for differences in rewards and transition dynamics across environments. We study knowledge transfer for offline reinforcement learning through a joint estimation framework that directly integrates source information into target value-function learning. We propose Direct Transfer Fitted QQ-Iteration (DFQI), which updates the target QQ-function while simultaneously borrowing the source information through an ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty that links the target coefficients to a weighted aggregate of source coefficients, with both determined jointly within each Bellman update. Using sieve approximation, we establish statistical guarantees for target estimation and policy learning in stationary discounted environments with common or heterogeneous transition kernels. Empirical studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DFQI framework in transferring source information to improve policy learning with limited target data.

Keywords: Offline reinforcement learning; Transfer learning; Joint estimation; Fitted QQ-iteration; Fused regularization.

1 Introduction

Many sequential decision-making problems call for learning effective policies from previously collected data. Examples include dynamic customer targeting in marketing (Simester et al. 2006) and adaptive treatment decisions in healthcare (Murphy 2003, Komorowski et al. 2018). We focus on the offline setting, in which policies are learned from a fixed dataset without further interaction with the environment during learning (Levine et al. 2020). Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a principled framework for studying such sequential decision problems, with policies evaluated by their expected cumulative rewards (Kaelbling et al. 1996, Sutton and Barto 2018).

In stationary, discounted Markov decision processes (MDPs), fitted QQ-iteration (FQI) provides a standard approach to offline policy learning (Ernst et al. 2005, Riedmiller 2005). It approximates the optimal action-value function through successive Bellman regressions, using observed transitions and the preceding QQ estimate to construct pseudo-responses. Then, the fitted QQ-function determines a greedy policy. From a statistical perspective, these updates involve estimating regression functions from a finite dataset of transitions (Murphy 2005, Clifton and Laber 2020). Limited target data can therefore constrain estimation accuracy, while collecting additional trajectories may be costly or impractical (Levine et al. 2020). Because successive regressions use estimated pseudo-responses, errors in one update can propagate to later updates and affect the value of the learned policy (Munos and Szepesvári 2008, Farahmand et al. 2010, Fan et al. 2020). These considerations motivate seeking additional information to improve estimation of the target QQ-function.

Transfer learning offers a way to address this limitation by using information from related source tasks to improve learning in the target task (Taylor and Stone 2009, Pan and Yang 2010). In many applications, such information is available in historical records from related populations or operating environments, but difficult to obtain from a small target sample alone. Statistical research on transfer learning has clarified when and to what extent related source data can improve target learning. In regression settings, theoretical guarantees characterize how these gains depend on source and target sample sizes and the similarity between tasks (Li et al. 2022, Tian and Feng 2023). In transfer QQ-learning, source data describe environments that may differ from the target in rewards, transition dynamics, and the distributions of observed states and actions. Accurate knowledge of a source environment does not, by itself, ensure improved policy learning in the target (Chen et al. 2026). The challenge is therefore to use shared information to improve estimation of the target QQ-function while accounting for differences relevant to the target policy.

A prominent strategy in statistical transfer learning follows a two-step design: a source-informed reference is first estimated, and target observations are then used to estimate a correction (Bastani 2021, Li et al. 2022). Although these methods provide theoretical guarantees, the reference remains fixed during the correction step, leaving any remaining mismatch with the target to be addressed through the correction alone. When task discrepancies are substantial, the reference may require a correction that is difficult to estimate accurately from limited target data (Tian and Feng 2023). In FQI-based transfer learning, this concern extends beyond an individual regression: errors remaining after correction can propagate through subsequent Bellman responses and affect the policy ultimately learned (Farahmand et al. 2010, Chen et al. 2026). These considerations motivate a statistical framework for transfer QQ-learning that jointly determines a source-informed reference and its target-specific correction within each Bellman update.

We introduce Direct Transfer Fitted QQ-Iteration (DFQI; Algorithm 1), a new statistical framework for incorporating source information into target QQ-function estimation. Its defining feature is to integrate information borrowing and target adaptation within a single joint optimization problem at each Bellman update. Each task constructs Bellman pseudo-responses from its own preceding QQ estimate. Under a common sieve representation, the joint objective combines the target and auxiliary source regression losses with an ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty on the difference between the target coefficients and a sample-size-weighted aggregate of source coefficients. The penalty encourages a sparse target correction to the source aggregate while retaining task-specific fitted functions. The resulting target QQ-function determines the final greedy policy.

For theoretical analysis, we consider the sieve implementation of DFQI, which approximates nonparametric QQ-functions through finite-dimensional basis expansions (Shi et al. 2022a, Chen et al. 2026). Under suitable regularity and transfer conditions, we first derive target estimation bounds for tasks with common transition kernels but potentially different reward functions. The bounds distinguish sieve approximation error, a statistical component governed by the combined source and target sample size, and a target-correction component depending on the available target data and the magnitude and sparsity of the aggregate discrepancy. We then extend the analysis to tasks with heterogeneous transition kernels under additional stability conditions. The resulting bounds retain the same structure, with the correction term accounting for discrepancies in both rewards and transition dynamics. In both settings, we trace estimation errors through the Bellman recursion to obtain value-loss bounds for the learned target policy, also accounting for the finite number of FQI iterations.

To complement the theoretical analysis, we conduct Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate target QQ-function estimation and a semisynthetic study based on real data to evaluate policy performance. The results provide empirical support for the effectiveness of DFQI with limited target data in the settings considered.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the related literature. Section 3 formulates the transfer learning problem, and Section 4 presents the DFQI framework and its sieve implementation. Section 5 establishes statistical guarantees under common and heterogeneous transition kernels. Section 6 presents the empirical studies, and Section 7 concludes. Proofs are provided in Appendix \thechapter.A.

2 Literature Review

Our study draws on two strands of literature: offline reinforcement learning and knowledge transfer. We first review statistical approaches to offline policy learning, then discuss transfer methods in regression and reinforcement learning.

Offline reinforcement learning.

Regression-based approaches provide a statistical foundation for learning policies from offline data, with fitted QQ-iteration serving as a basic algorithmic framework (Ernst et al. 2005). Analyses of fitted value iteration and QQ-learning relate function approximation and finite-sample estimation to policy performance, and examine how estimation errors propagate through successive updates (Murphy 2005, Munos and Szepesvári 2008, Farahmand et al. 2010, Fan et al. 2020). This literature provides tools for studying both individual Bellman regressions and the policies obtained from the resulting sequence of fitted functions.

A related line investigates the data coverage and function-class conditions required for statistically efficient offline learning (Chen and Jiang 2019, Xie and Jiang 2021, Foster et al. 2022). These studies clarify how learning guarantees depend on the interaction between the observed distribution and the representation of value functions. Pessimistic methods further incorporate uncertainty into value estimation and policy optimization, providing guarantees when offline data offer limited support for some decisions (Jin et al. 2021, Shi et al. 2022b).

Statistical approaches to long-term decision making also study policy optimization over prespecified policy classes under discounted- and average-reward criteria (Luckett et al. 2020, Liao et al. 2022). Complementary research develops methods for evaluating long-term policy values and conducting statistical inference in infinite-horizon settings (Shi et al. 2022a, Kallus and Uehara 2022). These contributions address policy construction, value estimation, and uncertainty quantification within an environment. Our study builds on these statistical foundations to examine how information from related environments can improve target QQ-function estimation and policy learning.

Transfer learning.

Statistical transfer learning studies the value of auxiliary data under explicit relationships between source and target distributions. Minimax analyses of nonparametric classification and regression characterize how task relatedness and sample sizes determine attainable target accuracy (Cai and Wei 2021, Cai and Pu 2024). In regression, a common principle is to borrow shared information while accounting for target-specific differences. Methods using proxy data, sparse linear models, and generalized linear models formalize this principle and establish conditions under which transfer improves target estimation (Bastani 2021, Li et al. 2022, Tian and Feng 2023). These studies motivate borrowing information through structured target adaptation, with transfer gains depending on both the information supplied by source data and the complexity of the adjustment required for the target.

Related developments address task heterogeneity through constrained estimation and fused regularization (Li et al. 2024, He et al. 2024, He et al. 2026). These constructions differ in their treatment of covariate shifts, regularization, and target adaptation; joint fitting can also precede a separate correction, as in TransFusion. This literature provides a foundation for borrowing information through joint estimation. Extending such constructions to FQI requires analyzing regression responses that depend on previously estimated value functions, as well as the policy learned through the resulting recursion.

Transfer learning for reinforcement learning.

Within RL, transfer methods differ in both the knowledge transferred and the data available for adaptation (Taylor and Stone 2009, Zhu et al. 2023). Successor features separate reward dependence from transition dynamics, enabling reuse of value information across tasks with common dynamics and different rewards (Barreto et al. 2017). Representation-based methods learn shared features from source tasks to improve downstream learning (Agarwal et al. 2023), and such benefits have also been established when both source and target learning use offline data (Ishfaq et al. 2024). Other approaches exploit shared structure in transition models (Chai et al. 2025b) or combine offline source observations with online target interaction when source and target dynamics differ (Qu et al. 2025). Our focus is on transferring information at the level of value-function regression using fixed offline datasets, with the target policy as the object of interest.

More directly related are methods that transfer information within Bellman regressions. Importance-weighted transfer FQI adjusts the contribution of source samples to account for differences in rewards and transition dynamics (Tirinzoni et al. 2018). Finite-horizon approaches combine backward regression with target-oriented response construction, including neural methods that reweight source transitions to accommodate differences in dynamics (Chen et al. 2025, Chai et al. 2025a). The closest work is Chen et al. (2026), which studies transfer FQI in stationary discounted environments. At each iteration, it forms task-specific Bellman responses, fits a pooled reference using target and source observations, and then estimates task-specific corrections. Its theory relates sample sizes and task discrepancies to learning accuracy while accounting for Bellman error propagation. Our contribution concerns the construction and estimation of the source-informed reference within each Bellman update. DFQI jointly estimates the target and task-specific source functions, using a weighted aggregate of the source functions as its reference. We establish statistical guarantees for this joint construction, characterizing how information borrowing and target correction affect target estimation and policy learning through the Bellman recursion.

3 Methodology

3.1 Statistical Formulation of Reinforcement Learning

We consider an infinite-horizon, time-homogeneous discounted Markov decision process (MDP) (Sutton and Barto 2018), specified by

ℳ={𝒳,𝒜,P,r,γ,ν}.\mathcal{M}=\{\mathcal{X},\mathcal{A},P,r,\gamma,\nu\}.

Here, 𝒳⊆ℝd\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} is the state space, with dd denoting the state dimension; 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a finite action space with mm actions, γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1) is the discount factor, and ν\nu is the initial-state distribution. At each time tt, the agent observes Xt∈𝒳X_{t}\in\mathcal{X}, selects At∈𝒜A_{t}\in\mathcal{A}, receives a reward RtR_{t}, and transitions to Xt+1X_{t+1}. Conditional on the current state-action pair, the distribution of the next state is independent of the preceding history and is determined by the transition kernel PP:

ℙ⁡(Xt+1∈B∣Xt=x,At=a)=P⁡(B∣x,a),B⊆𝒳​ measurable.\mathbb{P}(X_{t+1}\in B\mid X_{t}=x,A_{t}=a)=P(B\mid x,a),\qquad B\subseteq\mathcal{X}\text{ measurable}.

The conditional mean reward is r(x,a)=𝔼[Rt∣Xt=x,At=a]r(x,a)=\mathbb{E}[R_{t}\mid X_{t}=x,A_{t}=a].

A stationary Markov policy π\pi selects action aa in state xx with probability π⁡(a∣x)\pi(a\mid x). For a deterministic policy, π⁡(x)\pi(x) denotes the action selected with probability one at state xx. Writing 𝔼π\mathbb{E}_{\pi} for expectation under policy π\pi, we define the state-value and action-value functions by

Vπ​(x)\displaystyle V^{\pi}(x) =𝔼π​[∑t=0∞γt​Rt|X0=x],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}R_{t}\,\middle|\,X_{0}=x\right],
Qπ​(x,a)\displaystyle Q^{\pi}(x,a) =𝔼π[∑t=0∞γtRt|X0=x,A0=a].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}R_{t}\,\middle|\,X_{0}=x,\ A_{0}=a\right].

In Qπ​(x,a)Q^{\pi}(x,a), the initial action is fixed at aa, and policy π\pi is followed thereafter.

The optimal action-value function is

Q∗​(x,a)=supπQπ​(x,a),Q^{*}(x,a)=\sup_{\pi}Q^{\pi}(x,a),

and satisfies the Bellman optimality equation

Q∗(x,a)=𝔼[Rt+γmaxa′∈𝒜Q∗(Xt+1,a′)|Xt=x,At=a].Q^{*}(x,a)=\mathbb{E}\left[R_{t}+\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*}(X_{t+1},a^{\prime})\,\middle|\,X_{t}=x,\ A_{t}=a\right].

Equivalently,

𝔼[Rt+γmaxa′∈𝒜Q∗(Xt+1,a′)−Q∗(Xt,At)|Xt,At]=0.\mathbb{E}\left[R_{t}+\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*}(X_{t+1},a^{\prime})-Q^{*}(X_{t},A_{t})\,\middle|\,X_{t},A_{t}\right]=0.

This conditional moment equation states that the Bellman residual has conditional mean zero, providing a basis for regression-based estimation of Q∗Q^{*}.

Our goal is to improve estimation of Q∗Q^{*} for a target task by transferring information from related source tasks. Estimation of Q∗Q^{*} provides a basis for policy learning, since an optimal deterministic policy can be obtained as

π∗​(x)∈arg⁡maxa∈𝒜​Q∗​(x,a).\pi^{*}(x)\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*}(x,a).

In practice, we construct a greedy policy by replacing Q∗Q^{*} with its estimate.

3.2 Target and Source Data

We consider an offline transfer reinforcement learning setting with one target task and KK source tasks. The target task is indexed by k=0k=0, and the source tasks by k∈[K]={1,…,K}k\in[K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}. All tasks share 𝒳\mathcal{X}, 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and γ\gamma, but may differ in their transition kernels, mean reward functions, and initial-state distributions:

ℳ(k)={𝒳,𝒜,P(k),r(k),γ,ν(k)},k∈{0}∪[K].\mathcal{M}^{(k)}=\{\mathcal{X},\mathcal{A},P^{(k)},r^{(k)},\gamma,\nu^{(k)}\},\qquad k\in\{0\}\cup[K].

Let Q∗(k)Q^{*(k)} denote the optimal action-value function of task kk. For each task kk, we observe I(k)I^{(k)} independent trajectories, each containing TT transitions, collected under a behavior policy b(k)b^{(k)}. The resulting offline dataset is

𝒮(k)={(Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k),Ri,t(k),Xi,t+1(k)):1≤i≤I(k), 0≤t≤T−1},\mathcal{S}^{(k)}=\left\{\left(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)},R_{i,t}^{(k)},X_{i,t+1}^{(k)}\right):1\leq i\leq I^{(k)},\ 0\leq t\leq T-1\right\},

where ii indexes trajectories and tt indexes decision times. Thus, task kk contributes I(k)​TI^{(k)}T transition observations, which may be temporally dependent within each trajectory. The behavior policy satisfies

ℙ⁡(Ai,t(k)=a∣Xi,t(k)=x)=b(k)​(a∣x).\mathbb{P}\!\left(A_{i,t}^{(k)}=a\mid X_{i,t}^{(k)}=x\right)=b^{(k)}(a\mid x).

The target dataset 𝒮(0)\mathcal{S}^{(0)} is typically limited, while the source datasets {𝒮(k)}k=1K\{\mathcal{S}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} provide additional data from related tasks.

3.3 Similarity Between Target and Source Tasks

Following Chen et al. (2026), we characterize task discrepancies through differences in mean reward functions and transition kernels. For completeness, we also record the Bellman decomposition used in their task-similarity analysis.

Let ρ(k)​(x′∣x,a)\rho^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a) denote the density of the transition kernel P(k)(⋅∣x,a)P^{(k)}(\cdot\mid x,a). For each source task k∈[K]k\in[K], define the reward and transition discrepancies relative to the target task by

δr(k)​(x,a)\displaystyle\delta_{r}^{(k)}(x,a) =r(k)​(x,a)−r(0)​(x,a),\displaystyle=r^{(k)}(x,a)-r^{(0)}(x,a),
δρ(k)​(x′∣x,a)\displaystyle\delta_{\rho}^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a) =ρ(k)​(x′∣x,a)−ρ(0)​(x′∣x,a).\displaystyle=\rho^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)-\rho^{(0)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a).
Lemma 3.1 (Decomposition of action-value discrepancy).

For any source task k∈[K]k\in[K], define

δQ(k)​(x,a):=Q∗(k)​(x,a)−Q∗(0)​(x,a).\delta_{Q}^{(k)}(x,a):=Q^{*(k)}(x,a)-Q^{*(0)}(x,a).

Then

δQ(k)​(x,a)=\displaystyle\delta_{Q}^{(k)}(x,a)={} δr(k)​(x,a)\displaystyle\delta_{r}^{(k)}(x,a)
+γ∫𝒳maxa′∈𝒜Q∗(k)(x′,a′)δρ(k)(x′∣x,a)dx′\displaystyle+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*(k)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\,\delta_{\rho}^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)\,dx^{\prime}
+γ∫𝒳[maxa′∈𝒜Q∗(k)(x′,a′)−maxa′∈𝒜Q∗(0)(x′,a′)]ρ(0)(x′∣x,a)dx′.\displaystyle+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left[\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*(k)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})-\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*(0)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right]\rho^{(0)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)\,dx^{\prime}.

A short derivation is provided in the appendix. Lemma 3.1 relates differences in optimal action-value functions to reward and transition discrepancies and their propagated effects on future values. This motivates borrowing information across related tasks while accommodating differences in their QQ-functions. In the joint estimation procedure below, we implement transfer by regularizing the difference between the target candidate QQ-function and a weighted aggregate of the source candidate QQ-functions at each iteration.

4 Direct Q-Learning for Data Transfer

4.1 Direct Transfer Fitted Q-Iteration

The proposed joint transfer algorithm builds on fitted QQ-iteration for learning optimal action-value functions from offline data (Ernst et al. 2005). At each iteration, we construct each task’s Bellman pseudo-responses using its own preceding QQ-function estimate. The target and source functions are then jointly updated by minimizing their task-specific regression losses together with a penalty on the target correction relative to a weighted source aggregate. The source-informed reference and the target correction are thus determined within the same optimization.

For theoretical analysis, we partition the trajectories of each task into Υ\Upsilon disjoint groups of equal size, one for each iteration. For simplicity, assume that I(k)I^{(k)} is divisible by Υ\Upsilon for every task. Let 𝒮τ(k)\mathcal{S}_{\tau}^{(k)} contain all transitions from the trajectories in group τ\tau, used at iteration τ\tau. The number of transition observations from task kk at each iteration is therefore

nk=|𝒮τ(k)|=I(k)​TΥ,k∈{0}∪[K].n_{k}=|\mathcal{S}_{\tau}^{(k)}|=\frac{I^{(k)}T}{\Upsilon},\qquad k\in\{0\}\cup[K].

Here and below, (i,t)∈𝒮τ(k)(i,t)\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}^{(k)} means that the transition indexed by (i,t)(i,t) belongs to 𝒮τ(k)\mathcal{S}_{\tau}^{(k)}. Define the total source sample size and source weights by

ns=∑k=1Knk,wk=nkns,k∈[K].n_{s}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k},\qquad w_{k}=\frac{n_{k}}{n_{s}},\qquad k\in[K].

These source weights remain fixed across iterations. At iteration τ\tau, given the preceding estimates {Q^τ−1(k)}k=0K\{\widehat{Q}_{\tau-1}^{(k)}\}_{k=0}^{K}, we construct the pseudo-response for each task k∈{0}∪[K]k\in\{0\}\cup[K] as

Y^i,t(k),τ=Ri,t(k)+γ​maxa′∈𝒜​Q^τ−1(k)​(Xi,t+1(k),a′),(i,t)∈𝒮τ(k).\widehat{Y}_{i,t}^{(k),\tau}=R_{i,t}^{(k)}+\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{Q}_{\tau-1}^{(k)}\left(X_{i,t+1}^{(k)},a^{\prime}\right),\qquad(i,t)\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}^{(k)}. (1)

Let 𝒯(k)\mathcal{T}^{(k)} denote the Bellman optimality operator for task kk, defined by

(𝒯(k)​Q)​(x,a)=r(k)​(x,a)+γ​∫𝒳maxa′∈𝒜⁡Q⁡(x′,a′)​ρ(k)​(x′∣x,a)​d​x′.(\mathcal{T}^{(k)}Q)(x,a)=r^{(k)}(x,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\,\rho^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)\,dx^{\prime}.

Conditional on the preceding fitted functions, the corresponding population regression function is fτ(k)=𝒯(k)​Q^τ−1(k).f_{\tau}^{(k)}=\mathcal{T}^{(k)}\widehat{Q}_{\tau-1}^{(k)}. These pseudo-responses are held fixed during the current joint regression update. Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be a class of candidate action-value functions. For each task k∈{0}∪[K]k\in\{0\}\cup[K] and Q∈𝒬Q\in\mathcal{Q}, define the empirical Bellman regression loss

ℒτ(k)​(Q)=12​nk​∑(i,t)∈𝒮τ(k)[Y^i,t(k),τ−Q⁡(Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k))]2.\mathcal{L}_{\tau}^{(k)}(Q)=\frac{1}{2n_{k}}\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}^{(k)}}\left[\widehat{Y}_{i,t}^{(k),\tau}-Q\left(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)}\right)\right]^{2}.

Write 𝐐=(Q(0),…,Q(K))\mathbf{Q}=(Q^{(0)},\ldots,Q^{(K)}) and define the source reference by Q¯s=∑k=1Kwk​Q(k).\overline{Q}_{s}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}Q^{(k)}. Let ℛΔ,τ​(𝐐)\mathcal{R}_{\Delta,\tau}(\mathbf{Q}) be a regularizer for the target correction Q(0)−Q¯sQ^{(0)}-\overline{Q}_{s}. The joint update is

𝐐^τ∈arg​min𝐐∈𝒬K+1⁡{ℒτ(0)​(Q(0))+μ​∑k=1Kwk​ℒτ(k)​(Q(k))+λΔ​ℛΔ,τ​(𝐐)},\widehat{\mathbf{Q}}_{\tau}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{Q}\in\mathcal{Q}^{K+1}}\Bigl\{\mathcal{L}_{\tau}^{(0)}(Q^{(0)})+\mu\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\mathcal{L}_{\tau}^{(k)}(Q^{(k)})+\lambda_{\Delta}\mathcal{R}_{\Delta,\tau}(\mathbf{Q})\Bigr\}, (2)

where 𝐐^τ=(Q^τ(0),…,Q^τ(K))\widehat{\mathbf{Q}}_{\tau}=(\widehat{Q}_{\tau}^{(0)},\ldots,\widehat{Q}_{\tau}^{(K)}). Here, μ≥0\mu\geq 0 controls the contribution of the source regression losses, and λΔ≥0\lambda_{\Delta}\geq 0 controls the strength of transfer regularization. The source regression losses keep the source functions tied to their own Bellman pseudo-responses. Through the transfer penalty, the target regression loss can influence the source aggregate within the same update, allowing the reference to adjust as the target correction is estimated. Section 4.2 develops a sieve implementation of the joint update, in which the regularizer is an ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty on the correction coefficients. After Υ\Upsilon iterations, we use Q^Υ(0)\widehat{Q}_{\Upsilon}^{(0)} to estimate the target optimal action-value function Q∗(0)Q^{*(0)} and construct the corresponding greedy policy

π^Υ(0)​(x)∈arg​maxa∈𝒜⁡Q^Υ(0)​(x,a).\widehat{\pi}_{\Upsilon}^{(0)}(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{Q}_{\Upsilon}^{(0)}(x,a).

Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure.

4.2 Sieve Function Approximation for Direct Transfer FQI

We implement Algorithm 1 using a common sieve space for all tasks. By representing candidate functions as linear combinations of basis functions whose number can grow with the sample size, sieve approximation combines flexible function approximation with finite-dimensional estimation (Chen 2007). In our joint update, the common basis allows the weighted source reference and the target’s deviation from it to be expressed directly in terms of the task-specific coefficients. With the Bellman pseudo-responses held fixed, the squared regression losses and the ℓ1\ell_{1} correction penalty yield a convex optimization problem over the task-specific coefficients.

Let ϕ⁡(x)=(ϕ1​(x),…,ϕp​(x))⊤\phi(x)=(\phi_{1}(x),\ldots,\phi_{p}(x))^{\top} collect pp prespecified sieve basis functions on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. For notational convenience, label the actions by 1,…,m1,\ldots,m. Define the action-specific feature vector ξ⁡(x,a)=[ϕ⊤​(x)​𝟏​(a=1),…,ϕ⊤​(x)​𝟏​(a=m)]⊤∈ℝq,q=m​p,\xi(x,a)=\left[\phi^{\top}(x)\mathbf{1}(a=1),\ldots,\phi^{\top}(x)\mathbf{1}(a=m)\right]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{q},q=mp, where 𝟏​(⋅)\mathbf{1}(\cdot) denotes the indicator function. In the sieve implementation, we take 𝒬=𝒬p\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}_{p}, where

𝒬p={(x,a)↦ξ⊤​(x,a)​β:β∈ℝq}.\mathcal{Q}_{p}=\left\{(x,a)\mapsto\xi^{\top}(x,a)\beta:\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{q}\right\}.

For each task k∈{0}∪[K]k\in\{0\}\cup[K], a candidate action-value function therefore has the form

Q(k)​(x,a)=ξ⊤​(x,a)​β(k),β(k)∈ℝq.Q^{(k)}(x,a)=\xi^{\top}(x,a)\beta^{(k)},\qquad\beta^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}.

At iteration τ\tau, for each task k∈{0}∪[K]k\in\{0\}\cup[K], let Zτ(k)∈ℝnk×qZ_{\tau}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}\times q} denote the design matrix with rows

ξ⊤​(Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k)),(i,t)∈𝒮τ(k).\xi^{\top}\left(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)}\right),\qquad(i,t)\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}^{(k)}.

Stack the corresponding pseudo-responses in the same order to form

y^τ(k)=(Y^i,t(k),τ)(i,t)∈𝒮τ(k)∈ℝnk.\widehat{y}_{\tau}^{(k)}=\left(\widehat{Y}_{i,t}^{(k),\tau}\right)_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}^{(k)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}.

Under the common sieve representation, the source aggregate and target correction satisfy

Q¯s​(x,a)\displaystyle\overline{Q}_{s}(x,a) =ξ⊤​(x,a)​β¯s,\displaystyle=\xi^{\top}(x,a)\overline{\beta}_{s}, β¯s\displaystyle\qquad\overline{\beta}_{s} =∑k=1Kwk​β(k),\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\beta^{(k)},
Q(0)​(x,a)−Q¯s​(x,a)\displaystyle Q^{(0)}(x,a)-\overline{Q}_{s}(x,a) =ξ⊤​(x,a)​δ(0),\displaystyle=\xi^{\top}(x,a)\delta^{(0)}, δ(0)\displaystyle\qquad\delta^{(0)} =β(0)−β¯s.\displaystyle=\beta^{(0)}-\overline{\beta}_{s}.

We specify the transfer regularizer as ℛΔ,τ​(𝐐)=‖δ(0)‖1.\mathcal{R}_{\Delta,\tau}(\mathbf{Q})=\|\delta^{(0)}\|_{1}. Stack the task-specific coefficients as

θ=((β(0))⊤,…,(β(K))⊤)⊤∈ℝ(K+1)​q.\theta=\left((\beta^{(0)})^{\top},\ldots,(\beta^{(K)})^{\top}\right)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{(K+1)q}.

The joint coefficient update at iteration τ\tau is

θ^τ∈arg​minθ∈ℝ(K+1)​q{\displaystyle\widehat{\theta}_{\tau}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{(K+1)q}}\Biggl\{ 12​n0​‖y^τ(0)−Zτ(0)​β(0)‖22\displaystyle\frac{1}{2n_{0}}\left\|\widehat{y}_{\tau}^{(0)}-Z_{\tau}^{(0)}\beta^{(0)}\right\|_{2}^{2} (3)
+μ∑k=1Kwk2​nk‖y^τ(k)−Zτ(k)β(k)‖22\displaystyle+\mu\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{w_{k}}{2n_{k}}\left\|\widehat{y}_{\tau}^{(k)}-Z_{\tau}^{(k)}\beta^{(k)}\right\|_{2}^{2}
+λΔ‖β(0)−∑k=1Kwkβ(k)‖1}.\displaystyle+\lambda_{\Delta}\left\|\beta^{(0)}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\beta^{(k)}\right\|_{1}\Biggr\}.

Let β^τ(k)\widehat{\beta}_{\tau}^{(k)} denote the coefficient block of θ^τ\widehat{\theta}_{\tau} corresponding to task kk. The updated action-value estimates are

Q^τ(k)​(x,a)=ξ⊤​(x,a)​β^τ(k),k∈{0}∪[K].\widehat{Q}_{\tau}^{(k)}(x,a)=\xi^{\top}(x,a)\widehat{\beta}_{\tau}^{(k)},\qquad k\in\{0\}\cup[K].

For τ<Υ\tau<\Upsilon, these updated functions are used to construct the task-specific Bellman pseudo-responses at iteration τ+1\tau+1.

Proposition 1 (Convexity and solvability of the joint sieve update).

Fix an iteration τ\tau and condition on the preceding fitted functions. The joint update in (3) can be written as a generalized Lasso problem (Tibshirani and Taylor 2011):

θ^τ∈arg​minθ∈ℝ(K+1)​q⁡{12​‖y~τ−Z~τ​θ‖22+λΔ​‖D​θ‖1}.\widehat{\theta}_{\tau}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{(K+1)q}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\left\|\widetilde{y}_{\tau}-\widetilde{Z}_{\tau}\theta\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{\Delta}\|D\theta\|_{1}\right\}.

Here, y~τ\widetilde{y}_{\tau} stacks the task-specific pseudo-response vectors scaled to incorporate the regression weights, and Z~τ\widetilde{Z}_{\tau} is the correspondingly scaled block-diagonal design matrix. The contrast matrix DD maps the stacked coefficients to the target correction, so that D​θ=δ(0)D\theta=\delta^{(0)}. The objective is convex and admits at least one minimizer.

For brevity, the explicit constructions of y~τ\widetilde{y}_{\tau}, Z~τ\widetilde{Z}_{\tau}, and DD, together with the proof, are provided in Appendix \thechapter.A.2.

5 Theoretical Results

In this section, we study the statistical properties of DFQI (Algorithm 1) under sieve approximation. We first consider tasks with a common transition kernel and then extend the analysis to heterogeneous transition kernels under additional conditions. We begin by introducing the regularity conditions shared by both settings.

5.1 Common Regularity Conditions

Assumption 5.1.

The following conditions hold for the trajectory data.

  1. (i)

    Trajectory splitting. Complete trajectories are assigned to iterations independently of their observed values. Let 𝒟τ:=(𝒮τ(0),…,𝒮τ(K))\mathcal{D}_{\tau}:=(\mathcal{S}_{\tau}^{(0)},\ldots,\mathcal{S}_{\tau}^{(K)}) be the joint data block used at iteration τ\tau. The blocks 𝒟1,…,𝒟Υ\mathcal{D}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{D}_{\Upsilon} are mutually independent. The initial fitted functions {Q^0(k)}k=0K\{\widehat{Q}_{0}^{(k)}\}_{k=0}^{K} are fixed or constructed from an auxiliary sample independent of these blocks.

  2. (ii)

    Time-homogeneous dynamics. For each task k∈{0}∪[K]k\in\{0\}\cup[K], conditional on (Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k))=(x,a)(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)})=(x,a), the next state follows P(k)(⋅∣x,a)P^{(k)}(\cdot\mid x,a), with density ρ(k)(⋅∣x,a)\rho^{(k)}(\cdot\mid x,a) almost everywhere. The kernel does not depend on ii or tt. The logged data follow a stationary behavior policy b(k)b^{(k)} satisfying ℙ⁡(Ai,t(k)=a∣Xi,t(k)=x)=b(k)​(a∣x)\mathbb{P}\!\left(A_{i,t}^{(k)}=a\mid X_{i,t}^{(k)}=x\right)=b^{(k)}(a\mid x) for all i,t,ki,t,k.

  3. (iii)

    Stability and coverage. For each task k∈{0}∪[K]k\in\{0\}\cup[K], the Markov chain {Xi,t(k)}t=0T−1\{X_{i,t}^{(k)}\}_{t=0}^{T-1} has a unique stationary distribution with density μ(k)\mu^{(k)} almost everywhere and is geometrically ergodic as T→∞T\to\infty. Write ν(k)​(x)\nu^{(k)}(x) for the density of the initial distribution ν(k)\nu^{(k)}. There exist constants 0<cμ<Cμ<∞0<c_{\mu}<C_{\mu}<\infty such that cμ≤μ(k)​(x),ν(k)​(x)≤Cμc_{\mu}\leq\mu^{(k)}(x),\nu^{(k)}(x)\leq C_{\mu} for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and k∈{0}∪[K]k\in\{0\}\cup[K].

  4. (iv)

    Reward innovations. For each task k∈{0}∪[K]k\in\{0\}\cup[K], write Ri,t(k)=r(k)​(Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k))+ηi,t(k)R_{i,t}^{(k)}=r^{(k)}(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)})+\eta_{i,t}^{(k)}. Let ℋi,t(k)\mathcal{H}_{i,t}^{(k)} be generated by the initial state, observations through time t−1t-1, and the current pair (Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k))(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)}), immediately before (Ri,t(k),Xi,t+1(k))(R_{i,t}^{(k)},X_{i,t+1}^{(k)}) is observed. For every u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R},

    𝔼⁡[ηi,t(k)∣ℋi,t(k)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\eta_{i,t}^{(k)}\mid\mathcal{H}_{i,t}^{(k)}] =0,\displaystyle=0,
    𝔼⁡[exp⁡{u​ηi,t(k)}∣ℋi,t(k)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\{u\eta_{i,t}^{(k)}\}\mid\mathcal{H}_{i,t}^{(k)}\right] ≤exp⁡{ση2​u2/2},\displaystyle\leq\exp\{\sigma_{\eta}^{2}u^{2}/2\},

    where ση\sigma_{\eta} is uniform in i,t,ki,t,k. The Markov property holds relative to the same history: for every bounded measurable ff,

    𝔼⁡[f⁡(Xi,t+1(k))∣ℋi,t(k)]=∫𝒳f⁡(x′)​ρ(k)​(x′∣Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k))​d​x′.\mathbb{E}[f(X_{i,t+1}^{(k)})\mid\mathcal{H}_{i,t}^{(k)}]=\int_{\mathcal{X}}f(x^{\prime})\rho^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)})\,dx^{\prime}.

Condition (i) allows the current regression to be analyzed conditional on preceding fitted functions. Conditions (ii) and (iv) identify the Bellman conditional mean and control the residual fluctuations when those fitted functions are bounded. The density bounds in (iii) enter the norm comparisons used in the policy-value analysis.

  1. (i)

    Smoothness, bounded rewards, and approximation. For κ,c>0\kappa,c>0, let ℓκ=⌈κ⌉−1\ell_{\kappa}=\lceil\kappa\rceil-1.     Σ(k)=1T​𝔼​[∑t=0T−1ξ⁡(Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k))​ξ⊤​(Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k))].\Sigma^{(k)}=\frac{1}{T}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\xi(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)})\xi^{\top}(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)})\right].

For each task kk, let βr(k)∈ℝq\beta_{r}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{q} and βρ(k)​(x′)∈ℝq\beta_{\rho}^{(k)}(x^{\prime})\in\mathbb{R}^{q} be the action-stacked coefficients obtained by applying bpb_{p} to r(k)​(⋅,a)r^{(k)}(\cdot,a) and ρ(k)(x′∣⋅,a)\rho^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid\cdot,a), respectively. Conditional on the preceding fitted functions, define

βτ(k)=βr(k)+γ​∫𝒳maxa′∈𝒜⁡Q^τ−1(k)​(x′,a′)​βρ(k)​(x′)​d​x′.\beta_{\tau}^{(k)}=\beta_{r}^{(k)}+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{Q}_{\tau-1}^{(k)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\,\beta_{\rho}^{(k)}(x^{\prime})\,dx^{\prime}.

Lemma 5.1 (Uniform empirical Gram bounds).

Suppose Assumption 5.2(ii) holds and complete independent trajectories are assigned to iterations as described above. Let Jmin=min0≤k≤K⁡I(k)ΥJ_{\min}=\min_{0\leq k\leq K}\frac{I^{(k)}}{\Upsilon}. For a constant c>0c>0 independent of the sample sizes and sieve dimension,

ℙ⁡(⋃τ=1ΥℰΣ,τc)≤2​(K+1)​Υ​q​exp⁡(−c​Jminp).\mathbb{P}\!\left(\bigcup_{\tau=1}^{\Upsilon}\mathcal{E}_{\Sigma,\tau}^{c}\right)\leq 2(K+1)\Upsilon q\exp\!\left(-c\frac{J_{\min}}{p}\right).

The common approximation rule defines the task-specific Bellman coefficients in the same sieve coordinates. The lower density bound in Assumption 5.1(iii) gives Leb⁡(𝒳)≤cμ−1\operatorname{Leb}(\mathcal{X})\leq c_{\mu}^{-1}. Together with the approximation condition, this yields a Bellman approximation error of order p−κ/dp^{-\kappa/d} on the bounded-iterate event required in the theorems. Lemma 5.1 supplies the empirical spectral bounds needed for the joint fit under its sample-size condition. It uses independence across complete trajectories while allowing dependence within each trajectory.

5.2 Transition-Homogeneous Tasks

We first consider tasks sharing a transition kernel P(k)(⋅∣x,a)=P(⋅∣x,a)P^{(k)}(\cdot\mid x,a)=P(\cdot\mid x,a), while allowing task-specific reward functions. Write nall=n0+nsn_{\mathrm{all}}=n_{0}+n_{s} and nmin=min0≤k≤K⁡nkn_{\min}=\min_{0\leq k\leq K}n_{k}. For the joint update, take μ=ns/n0\mu=n_{s}/n_{0} and λΔ=cΔ​ns​log⁡q/(n0​nall)\lambda_{\Delta}=c_{\Delta}\sqrt{n_{s}\log q/(n_{0}n_{\mathrm{all}})}, where cΔ>0c_{\Delta}>0 is sufficiently large. Since the profiled correction loss has curvature of order κμ\kappa_{\mu}, its effective regularization level is λ¯Δ=λΔ/κμ=cΔ​nall​log⁡q/(n0​ns)\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta}=\lambda_{\Delta}/\kappa_{\mu}=c_{\Delta}\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{all}}\log q/(n_{0}n_{s})}. The quantity hΔh_{\Delta} measures the largest ℓ1\ell_{1} gap, over iterations, between the target Bellman coefficients and the weighted source aggregate; ss bounds the correction’s support size. Define the corresponding correction rate

Δs,hΔ=s​λ¯Δ∧hΔ​λ¯Δ∧hΔ.\Delta_{s,h_{\Delta}}=\sqrt{s}\,\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta}\wedge\sqrt{h_{\Delta}\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta}}\wedge h_{\Delta}.

For a target policy π\pi, write vπ,(0)=𝔼X0∼ν(0)​[Vπ,(0)​(X0)]v^{\pi,(0)}=\mathbb{E}_{X_{0}\sim\nu^{(0)}}[V^{\pi,(0)}(X_{0})] for its integrated value.

Theorem 5.1 (Policy value loss under homogeneous transitions).

Suppose Assumptions 5.1– 5.3 hold, all tasks share the transition kernel P(⋅∣x,a)P(\cdot\mid x,a), and the sieve basis consists of B-splines or wavelets satisfying the standard basis properties in Lemma E.1 of the supplementary material to Shi et al. (2022a). Let K,ΥK,\Upsilon be fixed and, for some deterministic constant B<∞B<\infty, assume

q⁡{log2⁡(nmin)+T​log⁡(q∨2)}nmin=o⁡(1),ℙ⁡(max0≤k≤K0≤τ≤Υ⁡‖Q^τ(k)‖∞≤B)⟶1.\frac{q\{\log^{2}(n_{\min})+T\log(q\vee 2)\}}{n_{\min}}=o(1),\qquad\mathbb{P}\!\left(\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq k\leq K\\ 0\leq\tau\leq\Upsilon\end{subarray}}\|\widehat{Q}_{\tau}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}\leq B\right)\longrightarrow 1.

Let π∗,(0)\pi^{*,(0)} be an optimal target policy. If max0≤k≤K⁡‖Q^0(k)‖∞≤Rmax/(1−γ)\max_{0\leq k\leq K}\|\widehat{Q}_{0}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}\leq R_{\max}/(1-\gamma), the greedy policy π^Υ(0)\widehat{\pi}_{\Upsilon}^{(0)} returned by Algorithm 1 satisfies

vπ∗,(0),(0)−vπ^Υ(0),(0)=1(1−γ)2​Op​(p−κ/d⏟sievebias+q/nall⏟pooledestimation+Δs,hΔ⏟target-sourcecorrection+γΥ​Rmax⏟iterationerror).v^{\pi^{*,(0)},(0)}-v^{\widehat{\pi}_{\Upsilon}^{(0)},(0)}=\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\,O_{p}\!\Bigl(\underbrace{p^{-\kappa/d}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{sieve}\\ \text{bias}\end{subarray}}\;+\;\underbrace{\sqrt{q/n_{\mathrm{all}}}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{pooled}\\ \text{estimation}\end{subarray}}\;+\;\underbrace{\Delta_{s,h_{\Delta}}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{target-source}\\ \text{correction}\end{subarray}}\;+\;\underbrace{\gamma^{\Upsilon}R_{\max}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{iteration}\\ \text{error}\end{subarray}}\Bigr).

Theorem 5.1 bounds the policy value loss by three statistical terms and an iteration remainder. The first term, p−κ/dp^{-\kappa/d}, arises from approximating the Bellman regression functions using the sieve basis. Increasing pp reduces this approximation error but also increases the coefficient dimension q=m​pq=mp. The second term, q/nall\sqrt{q/n_{\mathrm{all}}}, reflects the estimation accuracy supported by the combined target and source samples. The third term, Δs,hΔ\Delta_{s,h_{\Delta}}, accounts for correcting the discrepancy between the target and the weighted source aggregate. The final term, γΥ​Rmax\gamma^{\Upsilon}R_{\max}, represents the residual effect of initialization after Υ\Upsilon Bellman updates. The common factor (1−γ)−2(1-\gamma)^{-2} reflects error propagation through these updates and its effect on policy value.

The correction bound adapts to both the sparsity and the magnitude of the aggregate discrepancy. In the source-rich regime ns≫n0n_{s}\gg n_{0}, we have nall≍nsn_{\mathrm{all}}\asymp n_{s} and λ¯Δ≍log⁡q/n0\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta}\asymp\sqrt{\log q/n_{0}}, giving

Δs,hΔ≍s​log⁡qn0∧hΔ​(log⁡qn0)1/4∧hΔ.\Delta_{s,h_{\Delta}}\asymp\sqrt{\frac{s\log q}{n_{0}}}\wedge\sqrt{h_{\Delta}}\left(\frac{\log q}{n_{0}}\right)^{1/4}\wedge h_{\Delta}.

The first branch exploits the sparse support of the aggregate correction; the other two use its ℓ1\ell_{1} magnitude. Specifically, in the original definition of Δs,hΔ\Delta_{s,h_{\Delta}}, the linear branch applies when hΔ≤λ¯Δh_{\Delta}\leq\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta}, while the sparse branch applies when hΔ≥s​λ¯Δh_{\Delta}\geq s\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta}. Between these regimes, the correction rate is the geometric mean of the discrepancy magnitude and the effective regularization level.

This decomposition clarifies the distinct roles of source and target data. Once source data are abundant, the pooled estimation term continues to decrease with the combined sample size, whereas the regularization scale for target correction is primarily determined by n0n_{0}. For example, if additionally s​log⁡q=o⁡(q)s\log q=o(q), then q/nall+Δs,hΔ=o⁡(q/n0)\sqrt{q/n_{\mathrm{all}}}+\Delta_{s,h_{\Delta}}=o(\sqrt{q/n_{0}}). Thus, the estimation component of the bound can be smaller than the target-sample scale q/n0\sqrt{q/n_{0}}. A small aggregate discrepancy provides another favorable case through Δs,hΔ≤hΔ\Delta_{s,h_{\Delta}}\leq h_{\Delta}. The overall value bound may nevertheless be governed by sieve approximation or the finite-iteration remainder.

The bound retains the approximation, pooled estimation, and iteration rates of Chen et al. (2026). Under our structural conditions, the source-rich correction bound admits the branch s​log⁡q/n0\sqrt{s\log q/n_{0}}, improving the dimension dependence when s≪qs\ll q for a fixed action space. Moreover, hΔh_{\Delta} measures discrepancy relative to the weighted source aggregate, allowing differences across sources to offset one another. The discrepancy-dependent branches hΔ​(log⁡q/n0)1/4∧hΔ\sqrt{h_{\Delta}}(\log q/n_{0})^{1/4}\wedge h_{\Delta} also have counterparts in transfer regression (Li et al. 2022), reflecting a shared statistical structure: pooled observations support estimation across tasks, while target observations control the precision of discrepancy correction.

5.3 Transition-Heterogeneous Tasks

In the transition-heterogeneous setting, we consider tasks with transition kernels P(k)(⋅∣x,a)P^{(k)}(\cdot\mid x,a) and corresponding densities ρ(k)(⋅∣x,a)\rho^{(k)}(\cdot\mid x,a) that may differ across tasks. Reward functions r(k)r^{(k)} may also vary, so task heterogeneity arises from both immediate rewards and transition dynamics. Using the common sieve representations, define the discrepancy between source task kk and the target by

hk=‖βr(k)−βr(0)‖1+∫𝒳‖βρ(k)​(x′)−βρ(0)​(x′)‖1​d​x′.h_{k}=\left\|\beta_{r}^{(k)}-\beta_{r}^{(0)}\right\|_{1}+\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left\|\beta_{\rho}^{(k)}(x^{\prime})-\beta_{\rho}^{(0)}(x^{\prime})\right\|_{1}\,dx^{\prime}.

The weighted discrepancy hw=∑k=1Kwk​hkh_{\mathrm{w}}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}h_{k} summarizes heterogeneity in the underlying rewards and transitions. The earlier quantity hΔh_{\Delta} measures the largest aggregate Bellman-coefficient discrepancy over fitted iterations.

To control how differences between fitted value functions enter the Bellman coefficients, define the target transition coefficient operator 𝒦ρ(0)​g=∫𝒳g⁡(x′)​βρ(0)​(x′)​d​x′\mathcal{K}_{\rho}^{(0)}g=\int_{\mathcal{X}}g(x^{\prime})\beta_{\rho}^{(0)}(x^{\prime})\,dx^{\prime} and impose the stability condition

‖𝒦ρ(0)​g‖1≤Cρ​‖g‖L1,g∈L1​(𝒳),\left\|\mathcal{K}_{\rho}^{(0)}g\right\|_{1}\leq C_{\rho}\|g\|_{L_{1}},\qquad g\in L_{1}(\mathcal{X}), (4)

where Cρ<∞C_{\rho}<\infty does not depend on the sieve dimension. Retain the choices of μ\mu, λΔ\lambda_{\Delta}, and λ¯Δ\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta} from the homogeneous setting, and define the correction rate Δs,hw=s​λ¯Δ∧hw​λ¯Δ∧hw\Delta_{s,h_{\mathrm{w}}}=\sqrt{s}\,\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta}\wedge\sqrt{h_{\mathrm{w}}\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta}}\wedge h_{\mathrm{w}}.

Theorem 5.2 (Policy value loss under heterogeneous transitions).

Suppose Assumptions 5.1– 5.3 and the transition-coefficient stability condition (4) hold. Suppose the sieve basis consists of B-splines or wavelets satisfying the standard basis properties in Lemma E.1 of the supplementary material to Shi et al. (2022a). Let K,ΥK,\Upsilon be fixed and ns≳n0n_{s}\gtrsim n_{0}. For some deterministic constant B<∞B<\infty, assume

q⁡{log2⁡(nmin)+T​log⁡(q∨2)}nmin=o⁡(1),ℙ⁡(max0≤k≤K0≤τ≤Υ⁡‖Q^τ(k)‖∞≤B)⟶1.\frac{q\{\log^{2}(n_{\min})+T\log(q\vee 2)\}}{n_{\min}}=o(1),\qquad\mathbb{P}\!\left(\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq k\leq K\\ 0\leq\tau\leq\Upsilon\end{subarray}}\|\widehat{Q}_{\tau}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}\leq B\right)\longrightarrow 1.

Suppose all tasks use a common initialization β^0(k)=β^0(0)\widehat{\beta}_{0}^{(k)}=\widehat{\beta}_{0}^{(0)} for k∈[K]k\in[K], with ‖Q^0(0)‖∞≤Rmax/(1−γ)\|\widehat{Q}_{0}^{(0)}\|_{\infty}\leq R_{\max}/(1-\gamma). Let π∗,(0)\pi^{*,(0)} be an optimal target policy. Then the greedy target policy π^Υ(0)\widehat{\pi}_{\Upsilon}^{(0)} returned by Algorithm 1 satisfies

vπ∗,(0),(0)−vπ^Υ(0),(0)=1(1−γ)2Op(p−κ/d+q/nall+Δs,hw+γΥRmax).v^{\pi^{*,(0)},(0)}-v^{\widehat{\pi}_{\Upsilon}^{(0)},(0)}=\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\,O_{p}\!\Bigl(p^{-\kappa/d}+\sqrt{q/n_{\mathrm{all}}}+\Delta_{s,h_{\mathrm{w}}}+\gamma^{\Upsilon}R_{\max}\Bigr). (5)

Compared with Theorem 5.1, Theorem 5.2 retains the same approximation, pooled estimation, and iteration rates. The correction term is now characterized by hwh_{\mathrm{w}}, which summarizes weighted differences in rewards and transition dynamics between the source tasks and the target. The additional stability and common-initialization conditions allow these primitive differences to be controlled through successive Bellman regressions.

Under ns≳n0n_{s}\gtrsim n_{0}, we have nall≍nsn_{\mathrm{all}}\asymp n_{s} and λ¯Δ≍log⁡q/n0\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta}\asymp\sqrt{\log q/n_{0}}. A sufficient condition for the correction term to be no larger in order than the pooled estimation term is

n0≳hw 2​ns2​log⁡qq2.n_{0}\gtrsim\frac{h_{\mathrm{w}}^{\,2}n_{s}^{2}\log q}{q^{2}}.

Indeed, the middle branch then gives Δs,hw≤hw​λ¯Δ≲q/nall\Delta_{s,h_{\mathrm{w}}}\leq\sqrt{h_{\mathrm{w}}\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta}}\lesssim\sqrt{q/n_{\mathrm{all}}}, so the statistical part of the value bound is governed by sieve approximation and pooled estimation. For fixed sieve dimension and source sample size, this sufficient condition becomes more demanding as hwh_{\mathrm{w}} increases, highlighting the role of target observations in correcting task differences. The sparse branch s​λ¯Δ\sqrt{s}\,\overline{\lambda}_{\Delta} provides an alternative bound through the support size of the aggregate Bellman correction.

6 Empirical Studies

6.1 Monte Carlo Simulations

We conduct simulation studies to evaluate the effectiveness of DFQI (Algorithm 1) for offline transfer learning across related tasks. Following the simulation designs of Shi et al. (2022a), Chen et al. (2026), we consider the state space 𝒳=[−1,1]3\mathcal{X}=[-1,1]^{3} and action space 𝒜={−1,+1}\mathcal{A}=\{-1,+1\}. Starting from X0=tanh⁡(Z0)X_{0}=\tanh(Z_{0}), Z0∼N⁡(0,I3)Z_{0}\sim N(0,I_{3}), we sample actions uniformly from 𝒜\mathcal{A} and generate Xt+1=tanh⁡{0.75​diag⁡(At,−At,At)​Xt+ξt​𝟏3}X_{t+1}=\tanh\{0.75\operatorname{diag}(A_{t},-A_{t},A_{t})X_{t}+\xi_{t}\mathbf{1}_{3}\}, with reward Rt=At​Xt⊤​M​Xt+εr,tR_{t}=A_{t}X_{t}^{\top}MX_{t}+\varepsilon_{r,t}, where MM is the task-specific reward matrix and ξt\xi_{t} and εr,t\varepsilon_{r,t} are independent N⁡(0,0.52)N(0,0.5^{2}) noises.

Using this setting, we construct one target task (k=0k=0) and one source task (k=1k=1). The two tasks share the state transition mechanism, with task heterogeneity introduced through their reward matrices. The entries of the target matrix M(0)M^{(0)} are drawn independently, with Mi​i(0)∼N⁡(0,1)M_{ii}^{(0)}\sim N(0,1) and Mi​j(0)∼N⁡(0,0.252)M_{ij}^{(0)}\sim N(0,0.25^{2}) for i≠ji\neq j. For the source task, we set M(1)=M(0)+ΔM^{(1)}=M^{(0)}+\Delta, where Δi​j​∼iid​N​(0,σ2)\Delta_{ij}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^{2}). We vary σ∈{0.25,0.5,0.75,1}\sigma\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75,1\} to control task discrepancy and consider I(0)∈{20,40,60,80}I^{(0)}\in\{20,40,60,80\} target trajectories and I(1)∈{10,20,40,80}I^{(1)}\in\{10,20,40,80\} source trajectories, each of length five.

We compare three methods in our experiment: (i) No transfer, which applies FQI to the target data alone; (ii) batch QQ-learning, the two-step method of Chen et al. (2026), which pools source and target data and then estimates a target-specific correction at each fitted QQ-iteration; and (iii) Direct Transfer Fitted QQ-Iteration, our proposed DFQI method (Algorithm 1). All methods use discount factor γ=0.25\gamma=0.25 and an additive quadratic B-spline sieve with six basis functions per state coordinate and separate coefficients for each action. Initial coefficients are drawn independently from N⁡(0,0.012)N(0,0.01^{2}). In each replication, we estimate 𝔼​|Q^​(X,A)−Q∗​(X,A)|\mathbb{E}|\widehat{Q}(X,A)-Q^{*}(X,A)| by averaging over 200 test state–action pairs drawn independently from the initial state–action distribution, with Q∗Q^{*} approximated by Monte Carlo simulation.

Figure 1 shows that DFQI achieves lower median estimation error than both two-step batch QQ-learning and No transfer across all target and source sample sizes and task discrepancies considered. Its interquartile ranges are also generally shifted toward lower errors. These results support the effectiveness of DFQI in learning from source data under different degrees of task heterogeneity.

Increasing the target sample size reduces the median estimation error of all three methods, with diminishing gains. The reduction is largest when I(0)I^{(0)} increases from 20 to 40, smaller from 40 to 60, and more modest from 60 to 80. These equal increments of 20 trajectories correspond to progressively smaller proportional increases in target data, from 100%100\% to 50%50\% and approximately 33%33\%, respectively.

6.2 Real Data Analysis

We evaluate DFQI in a semisynthetic study based on adult sepsis data from MIMIC-III (Johnson et al. 2016). We use the preprocessed cohort selected following Komorowski et al. (2018) and adopt the evaluation framework of Chen et al. (2026).

States are constructed from 44 demographic and clinical variables in the preceding four-hour window and reduced to 10 principal components after transformation and normalization. Intravenous fluid volumes and vasopressor doses are each discretized into three levels, giving nine actions. Rewards combine penalties for deviations of 15 physiological measurements from prespecified ranges with a mortality-based terminal component (Prasad et al. 2017, Komorowski et al. 2018). At the end of each observed record, an additional reward of −50-50 is assigned for recorded 90-day mortality and +50+50 otherwise.

We retain only transitions between consecutive four-hour windows, yielding 218,298 transitions from 18,369 episodes. We designate adults aged 65 years or older as the target cohort and those aged 18–49 years as the source cohort, comprising 9,558 and 3,475 episodes, respectively. For each cohort, we calibrate an environment by estimating its reward function, transition distribution, termination probability, and initial-state distribution.

From each calibrated environment, we generate a fixed pool of 2,000 training trajectories under a uniform random behavior policy. In each replication, we sample I(0)∈{100,500}I^{(0)}\in\{100,500\} target trajectories and I(1)∈{250,500,…,2000}I^{(1)}\in\{250,500,\ldots,2000\} source trajectories without replacement. We compare the same three methods as in the Monte Carlo study, using quadratic B-spline bases with separate coefficients for each action and discount factor γ=0.6\gamma=0.6.

Generated trajectories contain at most four decisions, with earlier termination allowed. Each learned target policy π^\widehat{\pi} is evaluated by its mean discounted return over 200 newly generated target trajectories. We report policy regret vπ∗−vπ^v^{\pi^{*}}-v^{\widehat{\pi}}, where π∗\pi^{*} is an optimal target policy and vπv^{\pi} denotes the expected discounted return of policy π\pi in the calibrated target environment. Results are averaged across replications; lower regret indicates better performance.

Figure 2 presents the mean estimated policy regret vπ∗−vπ^v^{\pi^{*}}-v^{\widehat{\pi}} of the three methods across target and source sample-size configurations. With I(0)=100I^{(0)}=100 target trajectories, our proposed DFQI achieves lower regret than target-only FQI throughout the source-sample range and generally improves on batch QQ-learning, with the only exception at I(1)=1250I^{(1)}=1250 where their means are nearly equal. With I(0)=500I^{(0)}=500 target trajectories, DFQI has the lowest mean regret at every source sample size, with a clearer separation from batch QQ-learning. For both target sample sizes, the regret of the two transfer methods declines overall as more source trajectories are used, despite some nonmonotonicity. These findings illustrate the benefit of joint transfer for target-policy learning in the calibrated environment.

7 Conclusion

This paper develops Direct Transfer Fitted QQ-Iteration (DFQI) for offline reinforcement learning. At each iteration, DFQI integrates target and source QQ-function estimation within a single optimization problem, using an ℓ1\ell_{1} fusion penalty to share information across tasks while accommodating their heterogeneity. We establish estimation and policy regret bounds under sieve approximation for tasks with shared or heterogeneous transition kernels, clarifying the roles of sample size and task discrepancy. Monte Carlo simulations and a semisynthetic study calibrated to MIMIC-III illustrate the benefits of the proposed framework for QQ-function estimation and policy learning.

Appendix \thechapter.A Proof for Theoretical Results

\thechapter.A.1 Proof of Lemma 3.1

Proof of Lemma 3.1.

By the Bellman optimality equation, for the source task kk we have

Q∗(k)​(x,a)=r(k)​(x,a)+γ​∫𝒳maxa′∈𝒜⁡Q∗(k)​(x′,a′)​ρ(k)​(x′∣x,a)​d​x′.Q^{*(k)}(x,a)=r^{(k)}(x,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*(k)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\rho^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)\,dx^{\prime}.

Similarly, for the target task,

Q∗(0)​(x,a)=r(0)​(x,a)+γ​∫𝒳maxa′∈𝒜⁡Q∗(0)​(x′,a′)​ρ(0)​(x′∣x,a)​d​x′.Q^{*(0)}(x,a)=r^{(0)}(x,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*(0)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\rho^{(0)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)\,dx^{\prime}.

Subtracting the target Bellman equation from the source Bellman equation yields

Q∗(k)​(x,a)−Q∗(0)​(x,a)=r(k)​(x,a)−r(0)​(x,a)Q^{*(k)}(x,a)-Q^{*(0)}(x,a)=r^{(k)}(x,a)-r^{(0)}(x,a)
+γ∫𝒳[maxa′∈𝒜Q∗(k)(x′,a′)ρ(k)(x′∣x,a)−maxa′∈𝒜Q∗(0)(x′,a′)ρ(0)(x′∣x,a)]dx′.+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left[\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*(k)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\rho^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)-\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*(0)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\rho^{(0)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)\right]dx^{\prime}.

Adding and subtracting

γ​∫𝒳maxa′∈𝒜⁡Q∗(k)​(x′,a′)​ρ(0)​(x′∣x,a)​d​x′\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*(k)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\rho^{(0)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)\,dx^{\prime}

inside the last display gives

Q∗(k)​(x,a)−Q∗(0)​(x,a)=δr(k)​(x,a)+γ​∫𝒳maxa′∈𝒜⁡Q∗(k)​(x′,a′)​[ρ(k)​(x′∣x,a)−ρ(0)​(x′∣x,a)]​d​x′Q^{*(k)}(x,a)-Q^{*(0)}(x,a)=\delta_{r}^{(k)}(x,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*(k)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\left[\rho^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)-\rho^{(0)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)\right]dx^{\prime}
+γ∫𝒳[maxa′∈𝒜Q∗(k)(x′,a′)−maxa′∈𝒜Q∗(0)(x′,a′)]ρ(0)(x′∣x,a)dx′.\qquad\qquad+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left[\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*(k)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})-\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*(0)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right]\rho^{(0)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)\,dx^{\prime}.

Using the definitions

δQ(k)​(x,a)=Q∗(k)​(x,a)−Q∗(0)​(x,a),\delta_{Q}^{(k)}(x,a)=Q^{*(k)}(x,a)-Q^{*(0)}(x,a),
δr(k)​(x,a)=r(k)​(x,a)−r(0)​(x,a),\delta_{r}^{(k)}(x,a)=r^{(k)}(x,a)-r^{(0)}(x,a),

and

δρ(k)​(x′∣x,a)=ρ(k)​(x′∣x,a)−ρ(0)​(x′∣x,a),\delta_{\rho}^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)=\rho^{(k)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)-\rho^{(0)}(x^{\prime}\mid x,a),

we obtain the desired decomposition. ∎

\thechapter.A.2 Proof of Proposition 1

Proof.

Fix an iteration τ\tau. Conditional on the previous fitted iterates, the pseudo-responses {y^τ(k)}k=0K\{\widehat{y}_{\tau}^{(k)}\}_{k=0}^{K} are fixed. Let q=m​pq=mp, and define the stacked parameter

θ=(β(0)⊤,β(1)⊤,…,β(K)⊤)⊤∈ℝ(K+1)​q.\theta=\left(\beta^{(0)\top},\beta^{(1)\top},\ldots,\beta^{(K)\top}\right)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{(K+1)q}.

Define

Z~τ=diag(n0−1/2Zτ(0),μ​w1n1Zτ(1),…,μ​wKnKZτ(K)),\widetilde{Z}_{\tau}=\operatorname{diag}\left(n_{0}^{-1/2}Z_{\tau}^{(0)},\sqrt{\frac{\mu w_{1}}{n_{1}}}Z_{\tau}^{(1)},\ldots,\sqrt{\frac{\mu w_{K}}{n_{K}}}Z_{\tau}^{(K)}\right),

and

y~τ=(n0−1/2y^τ(0)⊤,μ​w1n1y^τ(1)⊤,…,μ​wKnKy^τ(K)⊤)⊤.\widetilde{y}_{\tau}=\left(n_{0}^{-1/2}\widehat{y}_{\tau}^{(0)\top},\sqrt{\frac{\mu w_{1}}{n_{1}}}\widehat{y}_{\tau}^{(1)\top},\ldots,\sqrt{\frac{\mu w_{K}}{n_{K}}}\widehat{y}_{\tau}^{(K)\top}\right)^{\top}.

Moreover, define the contrast matrix

D=[Iq,−w1​Iq,−w2​Iq,…,−wK​Iq].D=\left[I_{q},\,-w_{1}I_{q},\,-w_{2}I_{q},\,\ldots,\,-w_{K}I_{q}\right].

Then

D​θ=β(0)−∑k=1Kwk​β(k).D\theta=\beta^{(0)}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\beta^{(k)}.

Therefore the sieve joint update can be written as

θ^τ∈arg⁡minθ∈ℝ(K+1)​q​{12​‖y~τ−Z~τ​θ‖22+λΔ​‖D​θ‖1}.\widehat{\theta}_{\tau}\in\arg\min_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{(K+1)q}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\left\|\widetilde{y}_{\tau}-\widetilde{Z}_{\tau}\theta\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{\Delta}\left\|D\theta\right\|_{1}\right\}.

The first term is a convex quadratic function of θ\theta. The second term is also convex, since it is the composition of the convex norm ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} with the linear map DD. Hence the full objective is convex.

It remains to show existence of a minimizer. If λΔ=0\lambda_{\Delta}=0, the problem reduces to ordinary least squares with design matrix Z~τ\widetilde{Z}_{\tau}. Since the column space of Z~τ\widetilde{Z}_{\tau} is a closed subspace of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the projection of y~τ\widetilde{y}_{\tau} onto this column space exists. Hence the least-squares problem has at least one minimizer.

Now suppose λΔ>0\lambda_{\Delta}>0. Consider the linear map

A:ℝ(K+1)​q→ℝn0+ns+q,A​θ=(Z~τ​θ,D​θ).A:\mathbb{R}^{(K+1)q}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{0}+n_{s}+q},\qquad A\theta=\left(\widetilde{Z}_{\tau}\theta,D\theta\right).

Let

ℳ=A​ℝ(K+1)​q={(Z~τ​θ,D​θ):θ∈ℝ(K+1)​q}.\mathcal{M}=A\mathbb{R}^{(K+1)q}=\left\{\left(\widetilde{Z}_{\tau}\theta,D\theta\right):\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{(K+1)q}\right\}.

Because ℳ\mathcal{M} is a finite-dimensional linear subspace, it is closed. The original problem is equivalent to minimizing

Ψ⁡(u,v)=12​‖y~τ−u‖22+λΔ​‖v‖1\Psi(u,v)=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\widetilde{y}_{\tau}-u\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{\Delta}\|v\|_{1}

over (u,v)∈ℳ(u,v)\in\mathcal{M}.

Let {(uℓ,vℓ)}ℓ≥1⊂ℳ\{(u_{\ell},v_{\ell})\}_{\ell\geq 1}\subset\mathcal{M} be a minimizing sequence. Since

Ψ⁡(uℓ,vℓ)≤Ψ⁡(0,0)+o⁡(1),\Psi(u_{\ell},v_{\ell})\leq\Psi(0,0)+o(1),

we have

12​‖y~τ−uℓ‖22≤Ψ⁡(0,0)+o⁡(1),\frac{1}{2}\left\|\widetilde{y}_{\tau}-u_{\ell}\right\|_{2}^{2}\leq\Psi(0,0)+o(1),

and

λΔ​‖vℓ‖1≤Ψ⁡(0,0)+o⁡(1).\lambda_{\Delta}\|v_{\ell}\|_{1}\leq\Psi(0,0)+o(1).

Thus {uℓ}\{u_{\ell}\} and {vℓ}\{v_{\ell}\} are bounded. Since the ambient space is finite-dimensional, there exists a convergent subsequence, still denoted by {(uℓ,vℓ)}\{(u_{\ell},v_{\ell})\}, such that

(uℓ,vℓ)→(u∗,v∗).(u_{\ell},v_{\ell})\to(u_{*},v_{*}).

Because ℳ\mathcal{M} is closed, (u∗,v∗)∈ℳ(u_{*},v_{*})\in\mathcal{M}. By continuity of Ψ\Psi,

Ψ⁡(u∗,v∗)=inf(u,v)∈ℳΨ⁡(u,v).\Psi(u_{*},v_{*})=\inf_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{M}}\Psi(u,v).

Since (u∗,v∗)∈ℳ(u_{*},v_{*})\in\mathcal{M}, there exists at least one θ^τ∈ℝ(K+1)​q\widehat{\theta}_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{(K+1)q} such that

A​θ^τ=(u∗,v∗).A\widehat{\theta}_{\tau}=(u_{*},v_{*}).

Therefore θ^τ\widehat{\theta}_{\tau} is a minimizer of the original problem.

Finally, since the objective is convex, any minimizer satisfies the subgradient optimality condition

0∈Z~τ⊤​(Z~τ​θ^τ−y~τ)+λΔ​D⊤​∂‖D​θ^τ‖1.0\in\widetilde{Z}_{\tau}^{\top}\left(\widetilde{Z}_{\tau}\widehat{\theta}_{\tau}-\widetilde{y}_{\tau}\right)+\lambda_{\Delta}D^{\top}\partial\left\|D\widehat{\theta}_{\tau}\right\|_{1}.

Equivalently, there exists

z^τ∈∂‖D​θ^τ‖1\widehat{z}_{\tau}\in\partial\left\|D\widehat{\theta}_{\tau}\right\|_{1}

such that

Z~τ⊤​(Z~τ​θ^τ−y~τ)+λΔ​D⊤​z^τ=0.\widetilde{Z}_{\tau}^{\top}\left(\widetilde{Z}_{\tau}\widehat{\theta}_{\tau}-\widetilde{y}_{\tau}\right)+\lambda_{\Delta}D^{\top}\widehat{z}_{\tau}=0.

Writing

Δ^τ=D​θ^τ=β^τ(0)−∑k=1Kwk​β^τ(k),\widehat{\Delta}_{\tau}=D\widehat{\theta}_{\tau}=\widehat{\beta}_{\tau}^{(0)}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\widehat{\beta}_{\tau}^{(k)},

the subgradient satisfies

z^τ,j=sign⁡(Δ^τ,j)if ​Δ^τ,j≠0,z^τ,j∈[−1,1]if ​Δ^τ,j=0.\widehat{z}_{\tau,j}=\operatorname{sign}\left(\widehat{\Delta}_{\tau,j}\right)\quad\text{if }\widehat{\Delta}_{\tau,j}\neq 0,\qquad\widehat{z}_{\tau,j}\in[-1,1]\quad\text{if }\widehat{\Delta}_{\tau,j}=0.

Expanding the stacked KKT condition block by block gives

1n0​(Zτ(0))⊤​(Zτ(0)​β^τ(0)−y^τ(0))+λΔ​z^τ=0,\frac{1}{n_{0}}\left(Z_{\tau}^{(0)}\right)^{\top}\left(Z_{\tau}^{(0)}\widehat{\beta}_{\tau}^{(0)}-\widehat{y}_{\tau}^{(0)}\right)+\lambda_{\Delta}\widehat{z}_{\tau}=0,

and, for every k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K,

μ​wk​1nk​(Zτ(k))⊤​(Zτ(k)​β^τ(k)−y^τ(k))−λΔ​wk​z^τ=0.\mu w_{k}\frac{1}{n_{k}}\left(Z_{\tau}^{(k)}\right)^{\top}\left(Z_{\tau}^{(k)}\widehat{\beta}_{\tau}^{(k)}-\widehat{y}_{\tau}^{(k)}\right)-\lambda_{\Delta}w_{k}\widehat{z}_{\tau}=0.

This completes the proof. ∎

\thechapter.A.3 Proof of Lemma 5.1

This result supplies the empirical spectral bounds used below in the stochastic score analysis and the profiled curvature bound.

Proof of Lemma 5.1.

Fix τ\tau and kk, and let ℐτ(k)\mathcal{I}_{\tau}^{(k)} be the indices of the trajectories assigned to this iteration. Write Jk=|ℐτ(k)|=I(k)/ΥJ_{k}=|\mathcal{I}_{\tau}^{(k)}|=I^{(k)}/\Upsilon and

Wi(k)=1T​∑t=0T−1ξ⁡(Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k))​ξ​(Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k))⊤.W_{i}^{(k)}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\xi(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)})\xi(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)})^{\top}.

Then

Σ^τ(k)=1Jk​∑i∈ℐτ(k)Wi(k),𝔼​Wi(k)=Σ(k).\widehat{\Sigma}_{\tau}^{(k)}=\frac{1}{J_{k}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\tau}^{(k)}}W_{i}^{(k)},\qquad\mathbb{E}W_{i}^{(k)}=\Sigma^{(k)}.

The matrices Wi(k)W_{i}^{(k)} are independent across trajectories. The sieve-basis bound gives 0⪯Wi(k)⪯Cξ​p​Iq0\preceq W_{i}^{(k)}\preceq C_{\xi}pI_{q} for a constant CξC_{\xi}. Together with the population eigenvalue bounds in Assumption 5.2(ii), the matrix Chernoff inequality yields

ℙ⁡(λmin​(Σ^τ(k))<cG)+ℙ⁡(λmax​(Σ^τ(k))>CG)≤2​q​exp⁡(−c​Jkp).\mathbb{P}\!\left(\lambda_{\min}(\widehat{\Sigma}_{\tau}^{(k)})<c_{\mathrm{G}}\right)+\mathbb{P}\!\left(\lambda_{\max}(\widehat{\Sigma}_{\tau}^{(k)})>C_{\mathrm{G}}\right)\leq 2q\exp\!\left(-c\frac{J_{k}}{p}\right).

A union bound over kk and τ\tau proves the first claim. The stated growth condition makes its right-hand side tend to zero. ∎

\thechapter.A.4 Proof of Main Theorem

Homogeneous tasks: conditional regression.

We analyze the homogeneous update conditional on the fitted history, using the notation and tuning choices of Section 5.2. The argument proceeds from a one-step joint regression bound to the policy value loss in Theorem 5.1.

Let ℱτ−1\mathcal{F}_{\tau-1} be the sigma-field generated by the initial fitted functions and the data blocks 𝒟1,…,𝒟τ−1\mathcal{D}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{D}_{\tau-1}. Complete trajectories are assigned to iterations as in Assumption 5.1, so the current block 𝒟τ\mathcal{D}_{\tau} is independent of ℱτ−1\mathcal{F}_{\tau-1}. Write Yi,t(k),τ=Y^i,t(k),τY_{i,t}^{(k),\tau}=\widehat{Y}_{i,t}^{(k),\tau} for the pseudo-responses in (1), and define

fτ(k)=𝒯(k)Q^τ−1(k),ap=p−κ/d.f_{\tau}^{(k)}=\mathcal{T}^{(k)}\widehat{Q}_{\tau-1}^{(k)},\qquad a_{p}=p^{-\kappa/d}.

The reward-innovation and Markov conditions give

𝔼[Yi,t(k),τ∣ℱτ−1,Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k)]=fτ(k)(Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k)).\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y_{i,t}^{(k),\tau}\mid\mathcal{F}_{\tau-1},X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)}\right]=f_{\tau}^{(k)}(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)}).

Thus Yi,t(k),τ=fτ(k)​(Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k))+ei,t(k),τY_{i,t}^{(k),\tau}=f_{\tau}^{(k)}(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)})+e_{i,t}^{(k),\tau}, where the innovation is conditionally mean zero. Its conditional sub-Gaussian bound on the bounded-history event is verified in the proof of Lemma \thechapter.A.1 below.

The common approximation rule defines

βτ(k)=βr(k)+γ​∫𝒳maxa′∈𝒜⁡Q^τ−1(k)​(x′,a′)​βρ​(x′)​d​x′.\beta_{\tau}^{(k)}=\beta_{r}^{(k)}+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{Q}_{\tau-1}^{(k)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\,\beta_{\rho}(x^{\prime})\,dx^{\prime}.

These are the coefficients of the current Bellman regression approximants, conditional on the fitted history. Let Zτ(k)Z_{\tau}^{(k)} have rows ξ⊤​(Xi,t(k),Ai,t(k))\xi^{\top}(X_{i,t}^{(k)},A_{i,t}^{(k)}), and let yτ(k)y_{\tau}^{(k)} collect the current pseudo-responses. Then

yτ(k)=Zτ(k)​βτ(k)+rτ(k)+eτ(k),‖rτ(k)‖∞≲ap,y_{\tau}^{(k)}=Z_{\tau}^{(k)}\beta_{\tau}^{(k)}+r_{\tau}^{(k)}+e_{\tau}^{(k)},\qquad\|r_{\tau}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}\lesssim a_{p}, (\thechapter.A.1)

on the bounded-history event. The sieve-remainder calculation is given immediately below; eτ(k)e_{\tau}^{(k)} denotes the innovation and rτ(k)r_{\tau}^{(k)} the approximation remainder throughout.

With wk=nk/nsw_{k}=n_{k}/n_{s}, define the population and fitted aggregate corrections by

δτ,Δ(0)=βτ(0)−∑k=1Kwk​βτ(k),δ^τ=β^τ(0)−∑k=1Kwk​β^τ(k).\delta_{\tau,\Delta}^{(0)}=\beta_{\tau}^{(0)}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\beta_{\tau}^{(k)},\qquad\widehat{\delta}_{\tau}=\widehat{\beta}_{\tau}^{(0)}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\widehat{\beta}_{\tau}^{(k)}.

Assumption 5.3(i) bounds the population correction’s support by ss and its ℓ1\ell_{1} norm by hΔh_{\Delta}, uniformly in the fixed number of iterations. We first verify the sieve remainder and derive the profiled quadratic loss, with its projection form serving as an equivalent verification. Using the empirical Gram bounds proved above, we next control the stochastic scores and establish the one-step coefficient error bound. Finally, we convert this bound into Bellman residual control, propagate the residuals through FQI, and bound the greedy policy’s value loss.

Bellman sieve approximation.

We verify the remainder bound in (\thechapter.A.1) using the common approximation rule. By the approximation property in Assumption 5.2(i), for any function g⁡(x,a)g(x,a) satisfying g⁡(⋅,a)∈Λ⁡(κ,c)g(\cdot,a)\in\Lambda(\kappa,c) for every a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, let βg∈ℝm​p\beta_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{mp} stack the coefficients bp​(g​(⋅,a))b_{p}(g(\cdot,a)). Then

supx∈𝒳,a∈𝒜|g(x,a)−ξ⊤(x,a)βg|≤Cp−κ/d\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X},\ a\in\mathcal{A}}\left|g(x,a)-\xi^{\top}(x,a)\beta_{g}\right|\leq Cp^{-\kappa/d}

for some constant C>0C>0.

The coefficients {βr(k)}k=0K\{\beta_{r}^{(k)}\}_{k=0}^{K} and {βρ​(x′)}x′∈𝒳\{\beta_{\rho}(x^{\prime})\}_{x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}} defined above therefore satisfy

supx,a,k|r(k)(x,a)−ξ⊤(x,a)βr(k)|≲p−κ/d,\sup_{x,a,k}\left|r^{(k)}(x,a)-\xi^{\top}(x,a)\beta_{r}^{(k)}\right|\lesssim p^{-\kappa/d},

and, under the transition-homogeneous setting,

supx,a,x′|ρ(x′∣x,a)−ξ⊤(x,a)βρ(x′)|≲p−κ/d.\sup_{x,a,x^{\prime}}\left|\rho(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)-\xi^{\top}(x,a)\beta_{\rho}(x^{\prime})\right|\lesssim p^{-\kappa/d}.

By definition of fτ(k)=𝒯(k)​Q^τ−1(k)f_{\tau}^{(k)}=\mathcal{T}^{(k)}\widehat{Q}_{\tau-1}^{(k)}, we have

fτ(k)​(x,a)=r(k)​(x,a)+γ​∫𝒳[maxa′∈𝒜⁡Q^τ−1(k)​(x′,a′)]​ρ​(x′∣x,a)​d​x′.f_{\tau}^{(k)}(x,a)=r^{(k)}(x,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left[\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{Q}_{\tau-1}^{(k)}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right]\rho(x^{\prime}\mid x,a)\,dx^{\prime}.

On the bounded-history event, the preceding iterates have sup norm at most BB. The approximation bounds for r(k)r^{(k)} and ρ\rho therefore imply

supx,a,k|fτ(k)(x,a)−ξ⊤(x,a)βτ(k)|≲p−κ/d.\sup_{x,a,k}\left|f_{\tau}^{(k)}(x,a)-\xi^{\top}(x,a)\beta_{\tau}^{(k)}\right|\lesssim p^{-\kappa/d}.

Thus, βτ(k)\beta_{\tau}^{(k)} is the population sieve coefficient that approximates the one-step Bellman target 𝒯(k)​Q^τ−1(k)\mathcal{T}^{(k)}\widehat{Q}_{\tau-1}^{(k)}.

Direct profiling of the joint regression.

To analyze the penalized correction, we first eliminate the source coefficients from the joint quadratic loss. Fix an iteration τ\tau and condition on the preceding fitted functions. Write yτ(k)y_{\tau}^{(k)} for the held-fixed Bellman pseudo-response vector y^τ(k)\widehat{y}_{\tau}^{(k)} in the joint update, and use the regression representation

yτ(k)=Zτ(k)βτ(k)+rτ(k)+eτ(k),k=0,…,K.y_{\tau}^{(k)}=Z_{\tau}^{(k)}\beta_{\tau}^{(k)}+r_{\tau}^{(k)}+e_{\tau}^{(k)},\qquad k=0,\ldots,K.

For candidate coefficients, define

Lτ,k​(β)=12​nk​‖yτ(k)−Zτ(k)​β‖22,α=(β(1)⊤,…,β(K)⊤)⊤,B​α=∑k=1Kwk​β(k).L_{\tau,k}(\beta)=\frac{1}{2n_{k}}\|y_{\tau}^{(k)}-Z_{\tau}^{(k)}\beta\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\alpha=(\beta^{(1)\top},\ldots,\beta^{(K)\top})^{\top},\qquad B\alpha=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\beta^{(k)}.

The change of variables δ=β(0)−B​α\delta=\beta^{(0)}-B\alpha is one-to-one, with inverse β(0)=B​α+δ\beta^{(0)}=B\alpha+\delta. Hence the original joint update is the minimization over (δ,α)(\delta,\alpha) of

ℓτ​(δ,α)+λΔ​‖δ‖1,ℓτ​(δ,α)=Lτ,0​(B​α+δ)+μ​∑k=1Kwk​Lτ,k​(β(k)).\ell_{\tau}(\delta,\alpha)+\lambda_{\Delta}\|\delta\|_{1},\qquad\ell_{\tau}(\delta,\alpha)=L_{\tau,0}(B\alpha+\delta)+\mu\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}L_{\tau,k}(\beta^{(k)}).

For fixed δ\delta, the penalty does not depend on α\alpha. Define

α^τ​(δ)∈arg⁡minα​ℓτ​(δ,α),ℒprof,τ​(δ)=infαℓτ​(δ,α).\widehat{\alpha}_{\tau}(\delta)\in\arg\min_{\alpha}\ell_{\tau}(\delta,\alpha),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prof},\tau}(\delta)=\inf_{\alpha}\ell_{\tau}(\delta,\alpha).

The infimum is attained, since this is a finite-dimensional weighted least-squares problem. The correction component of any joint minimizer therefore satisfies

δ^τ∈arg⁡minδ∈ℝq​{ℒprof,τ​(δ)+λΔ​‖δ‖1}.\widehat{\delta}_{\tau}\in\arg\min_{\delta\in\mathbb{R}^{q}}\{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prof},\tau}(\delta)+\lambda_{\Delta}\|\delta\|_{1}\}. (\thechapter.A.2)

Conversely, any minimizer in (\thechapter.A.2), together with a corresponding α^τ​(δ^τ)\widehat{\alpha}_{\tau}(\widehat{\delta}_{\tau}), reconstructs a joint minimizer: its source coefficients are the blocks of α^τ​(δ^τ)\widehat{\alpha}_{\tau}(\widehat{\delta}_{\tau}) and its target coefficient is B​α^τ​(δ^τ)+δ^τB\widehat{\alpha}_{\tau}(\widehat{\delta}_{\tau})+\widehat{\delta}_{\tau}.

We now obtain the coefficient form of this profiled loss on ℰΣ,τ\mathcal{E}_{\Sigma,\tau}. Put

Aτ,k=Σ^τ(k),Ω^τ,s=(∑k=1Kwk​Aτ,k−1)−1,H^τ=Aτ,0+μ​Ω^τ,s.A_{\tau,k}=\widehat{\Sigma}_{\tau}^{(k)},\qquad\widehat{\Omega}_{\tau,s}=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}A_{\tau,k}^{-1}\right)^{-1},\qquad\widehat{H}_{\tau}=A_{\tau,0}+\mu\widehat{\Omega}_{\tau,s}.

Define the raw stochastic and approximation scores, and their source aggregates, by

gτ,e(k)\displaystyle g_{\tau,e}^{(k)} =1nk​(Zτ(k))⊤​eτ(k),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{k}}(Z_{\tau}^{(k)})^{\top}e_{\tau}^{(k)}, gτ,r(k)\displaystyle g_{\tau,r}^{(k)} =1nk(Zτ(k))⊤rτ(k),k=0,…,K,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{k}}(Z_{\tau}^{(k)})^{\top}r_{\tau}^{(k)},\qquad k=0,\ldots,K, (\thechapter.A.3)
sτ,e\displaystyle s_{\tau,e} =Ω^τ,s​∑k=1Kwk​Aτ,k−1​gτ,e(k),\displaystyle=\widehat{\Omega}_{\tau,s}\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}A_{\tau,k}^{-1}g_{\tau,e}^{(k)}, sτ,r\displaystyle s_{\tau,r} =Ω^τ,s​∑k=1Kwk​Aτ,k−1​gτ,r(k).\displaystyle=\widehat{\Omega}_{\tau,s}\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}A_{\tau,k}^{-1}g_{\tau,r}^{(k)}.

Write gτ(k)=gτ,e(k)+gτ,r(k)g_{\tau}^{(k)}=g_{\tau,e}^{(k)}+g_{\tau,r}^{(k)} and sτ=sτ,e+sτ,rs_{\tau}=s_{\tau,e}+s_{\tau,r}. Let ατ∗\alpha_{\tau}^{*} collect the source regression coefficients βτ(1),…,βτ(K)\beta_{\tau}^{(1)},\ldots,\beta_{\tau}^{(K)}, and write

δτ∗=δτ,Δ(0)=βτ(0)−∑k=1Kwk​βτ(k).\delta_{\tau}^{*}=\delta_{\tau,\Delta}^{(0)}=\beta_{\tau}^{(0)}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\beta_{\tau}^{(k)}.

For source perturbations u(k)=β(k)−βτ(k)u^{(k)}=\beta^{(k)}-\beta_{\tau}^{(k)}, let v=∑kwk​u(k)v=\sum_{k}w_{k}u^{(k)} and h=δ−δτ∗h=\delta-\delta_{\tau}^{*}. The target perturbation is then v+hv+h.

For a fixed aggregate perturbation vv, profiling the source quadratic loss subject to ∑kwk​u(k)=v\sum_{k}w_{k}u^{(k)}=v gives

min∑kwk​u(k)=v⁡μ​∑k=1Kwk​{12​u(k)⊤​Aτ,k​u(k)−gτ(k)⊤​u(k)}\displaystyle\min_{\sum_{k}w_{k}u^{(k)}=v}\mu\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\left\{\frac{1}{2}u^{(k)\top}A_{\tau,k}u^{(k)}-g_{\tau}^{(k)\top}u^{(k)}\right\} (\thechapter.A.4)
=μ⁡{12​v⊤​Ω^τ,s​v−sτ⊤​v}+Cτ,\displaystyle=\mu\left\{\frac{1}{2}v^{\top}\widehat{\Omega}_{\tau,s}v-s_{\tau}^{\top}v\right\}+C_{\tau},

where CτC_{\tau} does not depend on vv or hh. To see this, the constrained normal equations give Aτ,k​u(k)−gτ(k)=ℓA_{\tau,k}u^{(k)}-g_{\tau}^{(k)}=\ell for a common multiplier ℓ\ell. Stochastic score bounds.

We now control the stochastic scores. The infinity-norm bounds ensure penalty domination, while the Euclidean bounds control the pooled score contribution in target coefficient reconstruction.

Lemma \thechapter.A.1 (Concentration of the profiled stochastic score).

Fix an iteration τ\tau and condition on the previous fitted iterates. Use the raw and source-aggregate scores in (\thechapter.A.3). Under the sample-splitting, reward-noise, and profile-stability conditions, together with the conditions of Lemma 5.1, for each k=0,1,…,Kk=0,1,\ldots,K,

‖gτ,e(k)‖∞=Op​(log⁡(q∨2)nk),\left\|g_{\tau,e}^{(k)}\right\|_{\infty}=O_{p}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(q\vee 2)}{n_{k}}}\right),

and

‖sτ,e‖∞=Op​(log⁡(q∨2)ns).\left\|s_{\tau,e}\right\|_{\infty}=O_{p}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(q\vee 2)}{n_{s}}}\right).

The Euclidean scores also satisfy

‖gτ,e(k)‖2=Op​(qnk),‖sτ,e‖2=Op​(qns).\left\|g_{\tau,e}^{(k)}\right\|_{2}=O_{p}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{q}{n_{k}}}\right),\qquad\left\|s_{\tau,e}\right\|_{2}=O_{p}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{q}{n_{s}}}\right).

Moreover, the stochastic component of the profiled score satisfies

ζτ,e=𝒜τ,0​gτ,e(0)−𝒜τ,s​sτ,e,\zeta_{\tau,e}=\mathcal{A}_{\tau,0}g_{\tau,e}^{(0)}-\mathcal{A}_{\tau,s}s_{\tau,e},

and hence, under μ=ns/n0\mu=n_{s}/n_{0},

‖ζτ,e‖∞=Op​(ns​log⁡(q∨2)n0​nall).\left\|\zeta_{\tau,e}\right\|_{\infty}=O_{p}\left(\sqrt{\frac{n_{s}\log(q\vee 2)}{n_{0}n_{\mathrm{all}}}}\right).

If q→∞q\to\infty and cΔc_{\Delta} is sufficiently large, then

‖ζτ,e‖∞≤λΔ2\left\|\zeta_{\tau,e}\right\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\lambda_{\Delta}}{2}

with probability tending to one.
